newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - Bonn backs EU jobs plan if it's free - Waigel.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Bonn backs EU jobs plan if it's free - Waigel.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Monday Bonn would happily support greater European efforts to create employment so long as they do not cost money.

Germany and other European countries, in make-or-break efforts to rein in deficits this year to qualify for the single European currency, eschew new outlays and are looking for ways to to slash spending.

Addressing a perceived split between German and French policy on fighting joblessness, Waigel said policy coordination should focus on structural unemployment, and that much could be done without committing new funds.
"I do not believe that everything that could be effective in creating jobs costs money," Waigel told journalists during a meeting of European finance ministers.
Last month's election of a leftist government in Paris brought renewed emphasis on the jobs issue as Europe's number one economic policy issue.
At the Amsterdam summit, Paris succeeded in getting jobs measures made a formal part of the common programme, but the details have not been worked out and the plan has not been finally approved.
Waigel said European nations would benefit from greater coordination, comparing best practices around the continent, but should stop short of meddling in each others' affairs.
"Over-coordination should be avoided," he said, adding that Germany would not cede additional authority to Brussels.
Waigel noted a study by the International Monetary Fund showing that 80 percent of German unemployment is structural.

Even the current rebound to 2.5 percent economic growth this year and 3.0 percent next year is proving inadequate to the task of combating the current record levels of joblessness in Germany, he said.

Waigel said European monetary union would change the policy landscape by eliminating the buffer of flexible exchange rates, demanding that participating countries have greater flexibility in their labour markets.

While Waigel did not name names, southern European countries have had the reputation of resorting more easily to currency devaluations to boost growth and secure jobs, a policy option they will not have if they join EMU.
Waigel appeared concerned this could lead to higher payments to southern European countries to support social spending.
"Tensions cannot be allowed to result in higher transfers," he said.
What is needed, in Germany and elsewhere, is greater flexibility in labour contracts and employment practices, to allow employers to respond to fluctuating demand, Waigel said.
